Insurance translation services for industry professionals

November 4, 2023
Translation services | Financial translation | Professional Translation

Insurance translation is the translation of policies, claims paperwork and customer communications so that insurers, brokers and policyholders understand the same terms in any language.

It is specialist work, because one misread clause can change who pays for a loss.

If you work for an insurer, broker, loss adjuster or underwriter in the UK, you probably deal with customers, partners and claimants who do not read English fluently.

This page explains which documents need translating, what to look for in a provider and how to get a quote.

Which insurance documents need translation?

Insurance is document heavy, and nearly every document can need a translation at some point.

  • Policy wording, schedules and certificates of insurance.
  • Insurance Product Information Documents (IPIDs), key facts and terms of business.
  • Proposal forms, quotes and renewal notices.
  • Claim forms, statements, loss adjuster and surveyor reports.
  • Medical reports and expert opinions linked to personal injury or travel claims.
  • Reinsurance treaties, contracts and broker correspondence.
  • Complaint letters and final response letters.
  • Brochures, websites and marketing material for international customers.

Technical and legal material sits side by side in this list, so insurance projects often draw on legal translation, financial translation and, for medical reports, medical translation.

Why accuracy matters in insurance translation

Insurance language is exact, and many terms have no direct equivalent in another legal system.

Words such as excess, indemnity, subrogation, exclusion and warranty carry specific meanings under English law that a literal translation can distort.

Errors can lead to disputed claims, complaints and regulatory problems.

In the UK, the Financial Conduct Authority's insurance conduct rules (ICOBS 6.1.5R) require a firm to give customers appropriate information about a policy in good time and in a comprehensible form, so they can make an informed decision.

The rules also require an IPID for most consumer policies.

If your customer reads their policy in another language, an accurate translation helps you show that they could understand what they were buying.

Translating into UK English

If you receive documents from overseas insurers or brokers and need them in English, the target variety matters.

UK insurance uses its own vocabulary, such as excess rather than deductible, motor rather than auto, and buildings insurance rather than homeowners insurance.

A translator who writes in British English keeps your documents consistent with the rest of your UK policy and claims material.

Translation for claims and customer service

Claims are where language gaps do the most damage.

A claimant who cannot describe a loss clearly, or who misreads a request for evidence, can delay settlement and become frustrated with your service.

Translated claim forms, acknowledgement letters and settlement offers help you keep the process moving.

When claims handlers or loss adjusters need to speak to a claimant, a witness or a repairer, remote interpreting connects them with a professional interpreter by phone or video, without anyone travelling.

Confidentiality and data protection

Insurance files hold some of your customers' most personal information, including health, financial and property details.

You should expect any language provider to handle that data under UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, to limit access to those who need it and to sign a confidentiality agreement.

Ask where files are stored, who sees them and how they are deleted after the project.

Human translation, machine translation and insurance

Machine translation can help you understand the gist of an incoming email or a foreign claim form.

It is not a safe way to produce policy wording, settlement letters or anything a customer or regulator may rely on.

Insurance texts contain terms of art, long conditional sentences and numbers that machines can get wrong without warning.

Professional translators who specialise in insurance and finance know the terminology in both languages, and a second linguist can review the result before it reaches your customer.

How to choose an insurance translation provider

  • Check that translators have insurance or financial experience, not just general language skills.
  • Ask whether the provider keeps a glossary and translation memory for your terminology, so wording stays consistent across policies.
  • Confirm that a second linguist reviews each translation.
  • Ask about confidentiality, data security and file handling.
  • Ask whether the provider carries professional indemnity insurance, and what it covers.
  • Check that it can handle your file formats, such as PDF policy documents, Word templates and spreadsheets.

For documents that arrive as scans or PDFs, see how document translation works at BeTranslated.

Are you a translator looking for professional indemnity insurance?

This page is about translation services for the insurance sector, but many people search for cover for translators and interpreters.

The Chartered Institute of Linguists recommends in its code of professional conduct that practising linguists hold professional indemnity insurance.

That cover protects against claims for negligence or errors that cause a client financial loss.

Ask your professional body and a specialist insurance broker for current schemes and terms, because cover and premiums vary by provider and by your work.

Insurance translation with BeTranslated

BeTranslated supports insurers, brokers and other financial businesses with translation and interpreting in a wide range of language combinations, such as English to Spanish, French to German or any other pair you need.

For London-based projects, the London translation services page explains how BeTranslated supports businesses in the capital.

Every project is quoted per project, based on your document types, languages and volume.

To discuss your insurance translation needs, request a free, no-obligation quote.

Frequently asked questions

What is insurance translation?

It is the translation of insurance documents such as policies, claim forms and customer letters. The translator must preserve exact legal and technical meaning in the target language.

Which insurance documents are most often translated?

Policy wording, IPIDs, claim forms, loss adjuster reports and settlement letters are among the most common. Reinsurance contracts and marketing material for international customers also need translation.

Can you use machine translation for an insurance policy?

It can help you understand a document internally, but you should not rely on it for wording that customers or regulators may read. A specialist translator and a second reviewer reduce the risk of costly misunderstandings.

Do insurers need interpreters as well as translators?

Often, yes. Claims interviews, assessments and customer calls need interpreting, and remote interpreting lets handlers connect with an interpreter by phone or video without travel.

Do translators and interpreters need professional indemnity insurance?

The Chartered Institute of Linguists recommends that practising linguists hold it. It protects against claims arising from errors or negligence, so you can also ask your language provider about its cover.
